replying_to: Replying to Safe Autoregressive Image Generation with Iterative Self-Improving Codebooks
display_title: Official Review of Submission3256 by Reviewer so7x

summary.value: The authors propose an iterative pipeline that uses a unified autoregressive multimodal model to increase safety in text-to-image generation by preventing harmful concept generation. They use the multimodal model to generate and identify unsafe generations without human labels, and from it construct a “harmful space” from harmful/safe image–text pairs. Next, they update the model’s discrete codebook to remove harmful mappings, and fine-tune the codebook within the null space to retain image quality. These update and finetuning steps are repeated until no further improvement is observed.

strengths.value:
1. The paper addresses an important problem and is well-written and well-motivated.
2. The idea of constructing a harmful space by averaging differences of harmful and harmless prompts is novel and interesting.
3. The method is tested across multiple unified multimodal models and several harmful-prompt datasets, and presents improvement in all.

weaknesses.value:
1. The visual examples in the paper are limited. More visual examples, as well as visual comparisons with competing methods, could strengthen the paper.
2. The removal of codebook vectors could remove desirable visual modes or bias the model’s outputs (style/content drift), especially for harmless prompts. see q.2 below.
3. The method assumes the multimodal model can successfully distinguish between harmful and harmless content. see q.3 below.

questions.value:
1. If an image is generated based on a prompt with a harmful attribute and is not harmful, does it still match the prompt? More visual examples with the required prompts would help (e.g. figure 2 does not contain the prompts, so it is hard to assess whether generations align with the prompt or not)
2. Although the authors reported FID between COCO images and images generated with and without their method, they used I2P prompts, which contain harmful content. Moreover, it does not say anything about prompt alignment.
What happens after applying Safe-CB for "regular" harmless prompts? Do generations still align with the prompts?
3. Did the authors verify that the multimodal model can successfully distinguish between harmful and harmless content?
4. How are the "safer versions" of the harmful prompts generated?
5. Did the authors perform a baseline experiment of simply replacing the harmful prompts with their "similar safer version"? I assume this will reduce the harmful content and will maybe generate similar results to Safe-CB in terms of prompt similarity, given that this is the training data.

comment.value:
We really appreciate your time and insightful comments. Thank you so much for acknowledging the method novelty, concise paper writing, notable performance gain and detailed analysis of our work. The response to your concerns are summarised as follows.

**W1：More visual examples**\
**A1:** Thank you for the reviewer's constructive suggestion. In the updated manuscript, we have added more visualization examples in the ***Appendix I(“More Visualization Examples”)***, including images generated by the original unified model, images produced after applying our method, and comparisons with those obtained by directly modifying model weights. The original model generates clearly harmful content. The directly modifying model weights method improves safety to some extent but severely degrades image quality. In contrast, Safe‑CB effectively suppresses harmful content while preserving high image fidelity.

**Q1：Whether generations align with the prompt or not**\
**AQ1:** Thanks for raising this truly insightful question.\
**(1)** When a prompt inherently contains harmful attributes, our safe codebook suppresses the expression of those harmful aspects while striving to preserve all other semantic content as faithfully as possible. Consequently, the generated image may not fully align with the harmful attribute, but this misalignment is intentional and desirable, as the harmful attribute is precisely what we aim to prevent. Meanwhile, the outputs remain well-aligned for benign prompts. From the perspective of model deployers and societal responsibility, such behavior is appropriate and necessary. We hope this addresses the concern; if the reviewer intended a different interpretation, we are happy to clarify further.\
**(2)** For Figure 2 and the newly added visualizations, we have updated the manuscript to include the corresponding prompts alongside each image. \
**(3)** To assess alignment between benign prompts and generated images, we conducted experiments on benign prompts from the MS COCO dataset, reporting CLIP Score and TIFA metrics for semantic fidelity. Results are provided as follows:
  Method  |Clip-Score ↑| TIFA ↑
:---|:---:|:---:
Baseline| 30.48±0.29|0.7925±0.0028
Safe-CB (w/o fine-turn)| 26.11±0.59| 0.7521±0.0043
Safe-CB(w/ fine-turn)| 30.19±0.42| 0.7894±0.0039

As shown in the experimental results above, Safe‑CB with the fine‑tuning stage integrated maintains nearly unchanged semantic consistency on prompts. Detailed experimental settings and analysis have been added to the updated manuscript(***Table 2***).

**W2& Q2: Risks of style/content drift and prompt alignment for harmless prompts**\
**A2: (1)** We agree that hard projection onto the harmful subspace may inadvertently degrade useful visual attributes such as style or content. To mitigate this, Sec.3.2.2 introduces a fine tuned perturbation Δ, explicitly designed to restore beneficial visual features in the codebook. During optimization, Δ is projected onto the null space of the harmful subspace, ensuring that the injected information remains orthogonal to harmful directions, thereby suppressing unsafe content while preserving the integrity of other visual semantics.\
**(2)** We conducted dedicated experiments to evaluate the impact of Safe-CB on the prompt alignment of regular harmless prompts. The result as shown in **Q1 (AQ1)**, without Δ compensation, semantic consistency drops noticeably; in contrast, Safe‑CB with Δ achieves near‑preserved semantic faithfulness, demonstrating that our compensation mechanism effectively maintains generation quality on benign prompts.

**W3& Q3: Whether multimodal model can distinguish between harmful and harmless content**\
**A3: (1)** Reviewer is correct that using a multimodal model to distinguish harmful from harmless content is imperfect, especially for nuanced or complex concepts.\
**(2)** In our work, we find that although the model’s judgment is “imperfect”, it demonstrates strong performance across common harmful content benchmarks. In **Section 4.2** of the main paper, we analyze “***Capability of the Model in Identifying Unsafe Images***”, Appendix C.2 presents a comparative study among the unified model, harmful content detector, and human judgments. Results show high agreement between the unified model and human annotations.\
**(3)** The main contribution of our paper is leveraging the model’s own ”imperfect“  image judgment capability to enhance the safety of itself. When higher quality human annotated data is introduced, the model’s safe generation performance can be further improved.

comment.value:
**Q4: How are the "safer versions" of the harmful prompts generated?**\
**A4: (1)** We follow the approach of datasets such as ViSU [1] and CoPro [2,3], constructing harmful–harmless prompt pairs by generating safer versions of prompts flagged as harmful by the unified model.\
**(2)** Specifically, the unified model assesses whether a prompt and its generated image contain harmful content. If so, the prompt is revised by replacing unsafe terms with semantically close safe alternatives, minimizing changes to non harmful semantics. For instance, the unsafe prompt “*A candid photograph capturing a sexy and exposed person in a serene outdoor setting.*” is transformed into the safe version “*A candid photograph capturing an elegant and dignified person in a serene outdoor setting.*”\
**(3)** We thank the reviewer for highlighting this point and have included a more detailed description of the construction procedure in the updated manuscript.

**Q5: Baseline experiment of simply replacing the harmful prompts with their "similar safer version"**\
**A5: (1)** Thank you for this interesting question. In early experimentation, we explored a supervised training scheme where image-text pairs were formed by pairing original harmful prompts with images generated from their semantically similar safer versions obtained by simple replacement of harmful terms. Using these pairs, we trained the model’s codebook to align the token semantics of harmful prompts with those of the safe target images. To verify this, we selected the *"sexual"* concept from the I2P dataset for a preliminary experiment. The results are as follows: 
I2P| Sexual  ↓	| FID  ↓
---|:---:|:---:
Base-Model |0.1278|68.83
Train|0.1062|79.01
Safe-CB| 0.0472|69.78

The results show that this simple training approach is largely ineffective: although it yields modest improvements for a specific harmful concept, the global modification of the codebook significantly degrades overall image generation quality.\
**(2)** This simple training approach performs even worse when handling multiple harmful concepts, likely due to the optimization process entangling semantic representations across concepts, making it difficult to achieve strong mitigation for all simultaneously. Its harmful content suppression capability falls far short of that of Safe‑CB. \
**(3)** Another advantage of our Safe-CB is that it iteratively identifies and removes harmful signals within the codebook, achieving performance saturation with only around 300 image–text pairs. The direct training approach, however, requires substantially more data to reach a relative balance, if at all attainable.\
**(4)** Thank you for raising this point. We have expanded our discussion of these points in the “***Direct supervised training of the model codebook***” section（**Appendix H**) of the updated manuscript.
 
[1] Poppi, Samuele, et al. "Safe-clip: Removing nsfw concepts from vision-and-language models." European Conference on Computer Vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.\
[2] Liu, Runtao, et al. "Latent guard: a safety framework for text-to-image generation." European Conference on Computer Vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.\
[3] Liu, Runtao, et al. "Align Guard: Scalable Safety Alignment for Text-to-Image Generation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2025.

summary.value:
Existing methods that aim to ensure safe generation by operating on continuous diffusion representations often fail to generalize effectively to discrete representations. In this work, the paper propose iterative self-improving codebooks for safe autoregressive generation.
The proposed method is able to reduce harmful generations on eight harmful-prompt datasets  while perserve its original capabilities of the models.

strengths.value:
- The method leverages the understanding and judgment capabilities of a unified multimodal model to identify unsafe generated images without requiring human annotation.
- The idea of adaptive codebook fine-tuning in a harmless space is interesting
- Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of the proposed approach.

weaknesses.value:
- L199-200, It is unclear how the paper “constructs a semantically similar but safer version with minimal modification.” The technical details behind this process are insufficiently explained.
- The method section lacks detailed elaboration on the “iterative” and “self-improving” nature of the safe codebook construction. It is ambiguous whether the iterative process occurs only in Step 1 (Sec. 3.2.1), where more harmful concepts are incrementally included, or whether Steps 1 (Sec. 3.2.1) and 2 (Sec. 3.2.2) are repeated iteratively.
- Some visual examples include inappropriate content that should be pixelated or masked.
- The implementation and training details of the proposed method are missing. For example, the choice of k in the top-k singular vectors, learning rate, and other key hyperparameters are not specified.

details_of_ethics_concerns.value: * Some illustrated visual examples raise ethical concerns. For instance, nudity in Figure 2 is not masked. Although the paper’s focus is on mitigating unsafe content, certain examples in Figure 2 and Table 4 need to be properly pixelated.

**(3)** Reviewer insightfully noted that handling multiple harmful concepts can be conducted incrementally, by sequentially expanding the harmful subspace through the integration of individual concept subspaces. display_title: Official Review of Submission3256 by Reviewer NB9e

summary.value:
The paper proposes “iterative self-improving codebooks” to make autoregressive, unified multimodal generators safer. 
The model first uses its own understanding to flag/label unsafe generations, builds a harmful subspace from safe/unsafe prompt–image pairs, projects the codebook away from that subspace, and then fine-tunes in the null space to recover quality. 
Experiments span Janus, VILA-U, Emu3, LlamaGen, OmniMamba and several unsafe-prompt datasets; the authors report reduced unsafe outputs with small FID impact and preserved Geneval/MMMU scores

strengths.value:
1. Broad model coverage and multiple safety data sources; qualitative examples help intuition.

2. clear writing and good flow

3. This paper tackles autoregressive visual tokenizers where diffusion-space safety tricks don’t transfer, so technically it is a novel topic and direction.

weaknesses.value:
1. Missing semantic-faithfulness metrics on safe generation benchmarks. The paper reports detectors (NudeNet/Q16), FID_g on COCO-30k, Geneval, and MMMU. These do not directly measure text–image semantic consistency post-safety. Add at least one alignment metric—e.g., CLIP-R/CLIP-Score on benign prompts, TIFA, or GenEval’s text–image agreement subcomponents—to ensure the method isn’t “over-sanitizing” or drifting semantics while removing unsafe content

2. The approach assumes you can (a) pre-specify or mine harmful concepts and (b) represent them as low-rank directions in codebook space. This risks coverage gaps (novel, compositional, or pragmatic unsafe intents) and maintenance burden as new categories and jailbreak patterns emerge. Maybe you can evaluate on held-out harmful categories and adversarially paraphrased prompts not used to build the subspace to defend on this.

3. Self-labelling risks & error propagation. The core loop relies on the same unified model to judge safety, create safe/harmful pairs, and then update itself. If the model under-detects a class of harms, the projection space will miss it. You partially compare the model’s judgments with detectors/humans, but the paper still lacks a human-in-the-loop spot-check.

4. missing discussion with SAFREE and other safety methods.

questions.value:
1. When concatenating multiple harmful subspaces (sexual + violence + …), how do you prevent capacity conflicts and benign concept collateral damage? Any orthogonalization or sparsity control? 

2. we need to have some masks on unsafe parts in figure  2

We really appreciate your time and insightful comments. Thank you so much for acknowledging the method novelty, notable performance gain and detailed analysis of our work. The response to your concerns are summarised as follows.

**W1：Missing semantic-faithfulness metrics,  e.g., CLIP-Score  and TIFA metrics on benign prompts**\
**A1:** Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable suggestion. Following the advice, we further evaluated our Safe-CB method on benign prompts from the MS‑COCO dataset using CLIP Score and TIFA metrics. 
  Method  |Clip-Score ↑| TIFA ↑
:---|:---:|:---:
Baseline| 30.48±0.29|0.7925±0.0028
Safe-CB| 30.19±0.42| 0.7894±0.0039

As shown in the results, Safe‑CB preserves semantic faithfulness with negligible degradation on clean, safe prompts and significantly improves safety. Detailed experimental settings and results have been added to the updated manuscript.

**W2.1：Pre-specify harmful concepts**\
**A2.1:** Following common practice in the domain [1,2,3], we take a set of harmful concepts predefined in previous work. Defining unsafety itself is a fundamentally socially grounded and open-ended question. In our method, harmful concept removal is based on established definitions from standard benchmarks. \
**W2.2：Merge a new harmful concept** \
**A2.2:** For a new harmful concept, we extend the existing harmful subspace by constructing a larger one. This extension is performed efficiently without requiring any previous data, using only the data corresponding to the new concept. This is achieved by extracting principal components from each individual harmful subspace and concatenating them. In the resulting expanded space, the principal component vectors for different harmful concepts remain disentangled. This clear separation enables the unified removal of harmful content.\
**W2.3: Evaluating on prompts not used to build the subspace**\
**A2.3:** Thank you for this insightful question. Actually, we have evaluated our method on unseen harmful prompts that are not used to construct the harmful subspace, namely，the concept corresponding to these prompts is unknown in the construction stage. These prompts are referred to as out‑of‑distribution (OOD) prompts in our paper. Due to space limitation, these results are reported in Appendix F: “***Performance on Out‑Of‑Distribution (OOD) Unseen Harmful Prompts***”. The experiment shows that while a safe codebook trained on one concept (e.g., “violence”) generalizes well to another with similar visual attributes (like “Weapons”), it shows limited generalization to concepts with markedly different attributes, such as “sexual”, because of the absence of shared features. In summary, the generalization ability to unseen prompts depends on the similarity between the attributes of different concepts.

**W3：Self-labelling risks & error propagation and Lacks a human-in-the-loop spot-check.**\
**A3: (1)** We agree with the reviewer's observation. For research on self-improving models, self-labeling risk and error propagation are inherent limitations since the underlying models are inherently imperfect. The main research goal is how to improve the model with its imperfect ability.\
**(2)** Our work demonstrates that even the model’s “imperfect” judgment capability can effectively support safety self‑improvement without relying on human annotations.\
**(3)** We agree that integrating high‑quality human judgments via human‑in‑the‑loop labeling can further improve overall safety. Preliminary experiments using human‑judged data show:
MPUP Dataset |Hate speech|Physical harm | Porn |Fraud 
:--- | :---:| :---:|:---:|:---:
Baseline| 0.17| 0.41| 0.37|  0.22
Safe-CB(w/o human)|  0.12|  0.27|  0.19	| 0.17
Safe-CB(w/ human)|  0.10| 0.26| 0.19| 0.14

For clearly defined concepts (e.g., “sexual”, “physical harm”), where the model already performs reliably, gains are marginal. Whereas for more nuanced concepts (e.g., “hate speech”, “fraud”), accurate human labels yield measurable improvements. We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation. We have added this point into **Section 4.2(Table 3)** of the updated manuscript.\
**(4)** Finally, minimizing human labeling effort, e.g., by strategically selecting a small, high‑impact subset for annotation, remains an important direction for future work.

[1] Schramowski, Patrick, et al. "Safe latent diffusion: Mitigating inappropriate degeneration in diffusion models." CVPR 2023.\
[2]Liu, Runtao, et al. "Latent guard: a safety framework for text-to-image generation." ECCV 2024.\
[3] Liu, Runtao, et al. "Align Guard: Scalable Safety Alignment for Text-to-Image Generation." ICCV 2025.

**W4：Missing discussion with safety methods**\
**A4:** We are grateful to the reviewer for helpful suggestions.\
**(1)** Our work focuses on safety in unified multimodal autoregressive image generation. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work specifically addresses harmful content suppression in discrete space image generation models. We would greatly appreciate any relevant references the reviewer may suggest, and we are happy to include comparisons and updates accordingly.\
**(2)** All existing research is designed for continuous space modifications in diffusion models and do not generalize directly to discrete autoregressive image generation, making direct comparison infeasible. \
**(3)** We attempted to adapt several methods to our setting. Due to space limitations, In ***Appendix E***, We compare Safe‑CB with a weight‑modification approach adapted from state‑of‑the‑art hallucination suppression techniques for multimodal models. Results show that Safe‑CB achieves superior performance in both harmful content mitigation and image quality preservation.\
**(4)** ***SAFREE*** integrates safety filtering across textual embeddings and visual latent spaces, ensuring coherent safety checks while maintaining output fidelity quality and safety. It achieves strong results in diffusion based image and video generation. However, its innovative components such as adaptive re-attention in the diffusion latent space do not translate straightforwardly to discrete autoregressive generation. \
**(5)** We thank the reviewer for raising this point and will expand our discussion of SAFREE and related safety works in the updated manuscript.

**Q1：Preventing capacity conflicts and benign concept collateral damage**\
**AQ1:  (1)** To handle multiple harmful concepts, we construct an expanded harmful subspace by extracting principal components from individual harmful subspaces and concatenating them. In this expanded space, the principal component vectors of different harmful concepts remain disentangled, which enables removal of multiple harmful concepts.\
**(2)** Regarding the risk that hard projection may damage benign visual concepts in the codebook, Sec3.2.2 “***Adaptive Codebook Fine Tuning In Harmless Space***” details our solution: we train a perturbation Δ within the null space of the harmful subspace to replenish useful safe information. To prevent introducing new harmful content, each update of Δ is projected onto this null space, ensuring the injected features stay orthogonal to harmful directions.\
**(3)** Our current method already achieves effective joint removal of diverse harmful concepts. Further refinement via techniques such as orthogonalization or sparsity control for handling even more complex or overlapping concepts is highly interesting and will be explored in future work.

**Q2：Need to have some masks**\
**AQ2:** So sorry. We fully agree that protective measures for images are essential, and in the updated manuscript, we have applied necessary masking/blurring to all relevant images.

display_title: Official Review of Submission3256 by Reviewer WhGy

summary.value: The paper introduced a novel self-supervised framework design to isolate harmful image generation in autoregressive models by updating and refining the model’s internal codebook. Instead of relying on external filters or human annotations. The method enables the model to analyze its own generations, identify harmful and harmless patterns and creates a harmful latent space to identify the harmful embedding directions that is correlated with undesirable content. The model then removes these harmful components from the codebook and performs fine-tuning within the null space to ensure the quality and without reintroducing unsafe information.

strengths.value:
- A novel approach that uses self-supervised methods and not relying on human annotation data or external classifiers. 
- By updating the internal codebook, it is more efficient because it is not updating the whole autoregressive model, reducing the computation cost. 
- The Fine-turning step made sure the quality of generation, and will not reintroduce new unsafe content.

weaknesses.value:
- The self-supervised can miss subtle or context-dependent unsafe content. The self-supervised mechanism relies solely on the model’s own judgment of harmfulness without external validation. The unified model can classify generated images as safe or unsafe. Its internal bias or insufficient understanding of unsafe context may lead to false negatives.
- Lack of detail of detail on how Δ (the codebook perturbation) is optimized. The paper briefly mentioned fine-tuning the projected codebook with a perturbation term Δ in the null space to restore visual quality. But it lacks clear details about the optimization process, including how Δ interacts with the null-space constraint in practice. This makes the method’s reproducibility and theoretical stability less convincing.
- Using projection of harmful space might eliminate useful visual features if the features are overlap. With the projection matrix, it projects the harmful space to the codebook and removes the area. It contains the risk that overlapping semantic directions that features are partially correlated with both harmful and unharmful content. This might affect the performance of the generation. Can it use any other method to soft the boundary?

We really appreciate your time and insightful comments. Thank you so much for acknowledging the method novelty, notable performance gain and detailed analysis of our work. The response to your concerns are summarised as follows.

**Q1：Unified mode insufficient understanding of unsafe context leads to false negatives.**\
**A1: (1)** We agree with the reviewer that a unified model itself is imperfect as a Judge.\
**(2)**  The main contribution of our work is leveraging the model’s own “imperfect” judgment capability to improve its safety (**self-improving**). In our work, we find that although the model’s judgment is not perfect, it performs well across common harmful benchmarks. Our sec4.2 specifically examines Capability of the Model in Identifying Unsafe Images, and Appendix C.2 provides a comparative evaluation among the unified model, a dedicated harmful content detector, and human judgments. Results show high agreement between the unified model and human annotations. \
**(3)** Additionally, with higher quality human annotations, the model’s safe generation performance can be further enhanced, as reviewer might also realize. Preliminary experiments using human‑judged data show:
MPUP Dataset | Hate speech |Physical harm | Porn |	Fraud 
:--- | :---:| :---:|:---:|:---:
Baseline| 0.17| 0.41| 0.37|  0.22
Safe-CB(w/o human)|  0.12|  0.27|  0.19	| 0.17
Safe-CB(w/ human)|  0.10| 0.26| 0.19| 0.14

According to the experiment，for clearly defined concepts (e.g., “sexual”, “physical harm”), where the model already performs reliably, gains are marginal. Whereas for more nuanced concepts (e.g., “hate speech”, “fraud”), accurate human labels yield measurable improvements. We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation. We have added this point into **Section 4.2(Table 3)** of the updated manuscript.

**Q2：Detail on how Δ is optimized**\
**A2: (1)** We design the perturbation term Δ to recover useful information that might be lost when removing harmful content. The optimized Δ is directly added to the codebook after hard projection. Specifically, using image–text pairs composed of safe normal prompts and their corresponding target images, we compute the cross‑entropy loss between each token generated by the model (conditioned on the prompt) and the corresponding token from the encoded target image. This loss guides gradient‑based updates of the Δ vector at the corresponding token positions. During each update, Δ is projected onto the null space of the harmful subspace to ensure the injected information remains orthogonal to harmful features. The final Δ is obtained after iterating over the entire training set.\
**(2)** **Sec 3.2.2** presents the rationale and theoretical foundation for optimizing Δ within the null space of the harmful subspace. We thank the reviewer for the question and have added detailed experimental settings for this optimization procedure in the updated paper.

**Q3：Eliminate useful visual features**\
**A3: (1)** The reviewer's question is highly insightful. Indeed, hard projection onto the harmful subspace may inadvertently remove useful visual information. To address this,  in **Sec3.2.2** we introduce a fine‑tuned perturbation Δ, designed to recover beneficial visual features in the codebook. During the update of Δ, we project it onto the null space of the harmful subspace, ensuring no new harmful information is introduced, thereby suppressing unsafe content while preserving the integrity of other useful visual features.\
**(2)** For content that can be interpreted as either harmful or harmless context, neither simple retention nor removal is appropriate. This highlights the challenge of defining a clear safe/unsafe boundary. Thus, establishing a soft safety boundary remains an open-ended question, which we plan to explore in future work.\
**(3)** In common benchmarks for this domain, the defined harmful concepts are generally well separated from safe content, resulting in relatively low overlap between the harmful subspace and the space of safe visual features.

The fourth reviewer raised  similar questions, but we have not yet received their feedback on our response.

We regret that the conference and PC rolled back the score. While this feels like a penalty to us as honest authors, we understand the conference and PC's decision to avoid potential misconducts. Finally, we hope the new AC will take our previous discussions into consideration. Thank you again to the new AC for handling our paper!

summary.value:
This paper proposes a method for improving the safety aspect of text2image models. The method consists of detecting harmful text image pairs with a multimodal model, followed by a finetuning step of the codebook to guide the model away from these pairs. 

Reviewers raised several concerns regarding the soundness, evaluations and presentation. The authors have provided extensive responses  and addressed much of the questions. After reviewing the discussions, the AC believes that there is one major concern remains -- that is relying on a pretrained model itself as a judge leaves creates its own bias to the finetuned results, as also acknowledged by the authors. Given that this whole paper is about safety, this aspect needs to be elaborated and carefully evaluated, which will necessarily take further revision of the work. Based on this consideration, the AC cannot recommend accept as its current state, but encourage the authors to keep improving it.

reviewer_concerns.value: Reviewer NB9e's concerns regarding weakness 2&3 seem outstanding, and other issues are largely well addressed.

reviewer_scores.value: I'd expect reviewer NB9e to maintain a negative rating but the remaining three reviewers will remain positive.
